title: Chapter 209 – The Bell Without a Sound
html:
[Terrace Four – Mo Yan]

The first thing Mo Yan learns about silence is that it has a texture.

It is not nothing. Nothing would be easy. Nothing is what she knew in the cart-house at the back of the Quiet Remedy's hospice, in the nights before words, when the whole world was a wet cloth held over her mouth. This is different. The silence of the Fourth Terrace is thick and patient and faintly warm, like the inside of a mitten, and it presses on her eardrums with a gentle insistence, the way a hand presses on the back of a child who has been told to wait.

She has been awake in it for eleven hours.

Jian is asleep on a bench inside the Cartographer's shed, sitting up, his chin on his chest and his shaking hand tucked into his sleeve. Hua sits cross-legged on the floor beside the stove, with her eyes shut and her mark-hand resting on her knee. She is not sleeping. She is listening, and what she is listening to is a woman who has been silent for six hundred years and is, even now, thinking about whether to end the world. Every few minutes Hua's mouth tightens, and Mo Yan knows that the thing at the other end of the mark has said something.

The Cartographer has gone out. He said, in his creaking, kindly way, that he had maps to tend. Mo Yan does not believe him. She thinks he has gone to sit with the sleeping Keepers, as he does each night, and speak to them without speaking.

She holds the black glass bell in both hands.

It is small, no bigger than a plum, and so dark it seems to drink the lamp. The Ferryman gave it to her in the last hour of his life, and he said it was the first fare, the girl of nine whose year of life had paid for the first crossing of the first boat, and that the girl's voice was in it. Mo Yan has not rung it. She has been afraid to. Everything she has ever rung, or sung, or said, has cost someone something.

But she has been sitting for eleven hours, and the stone girl is out there in the dust with her mouth open on a word, and the forty hours are down to twenty-nine.

She gets up.

---

The Terrace at night is a place of long blue shadows and the pale smear of the sky. The stone Keepers stand in their rows, four hundred of them, each one a different height, in a different posture of leaning or listening. None of them is carved. That is what unsettles Mo Yan most. They are not statues. They are people who stopped, and the stopping has gone all the way through, like frost through a pond, and in the places where a hand once touched a sleeve she can still see the creases.

She walks between them with the bell held against her chest.

The Quay of Bells lies at the Terrace's lower edge, a long curved platform of fitted slabs, empty now except for six figures. Six of Ming Xue's pupils stand in a ragged line at the lip, facing the stairs they climbed to get here. Their robes are the pale blue of the Azure Cloud Sect and the stone has taken the blue and turned it to the color of a bruise. The girl at the end is the youngest. Her braid is stone, and so is the ribbon in it. One hand is lifted halfway to her mouth, as though she was about to cover a laugh.

Mo Yan stops in front of her.

She is perhaps fifteen. She has a round, ordinary face, a little flat across the nose, and her eyes are open. The stone has not closed them. They are an ordinary brown, and the light in them is not the light of a statue. It is the light of a person at the bottom of a well, looking up.

"I know you can hear me," Mo Yan says.

She says it very quietly. She says it in the half-whisper of a child who is not sure she is allowed. And nothing happens. No chill climbs her throat. No stone creeps up her tongue. The Terrace swallows the sound the way the sea swallows a pebble, and she stands in the blue dark with her breath going in and out and understands, with a small shock, that a whisper is not a threat.

It is the loud things that wake the ground. Jian told her that. The Cartographer's lid will hold against a murmur, not a shout. Hua's thoughts pass through the mark like a held breath through a straw. The Terrace does not hate speech. It hates force. It hates the thing that pushes a voice outward.

And a song is a push. A song is the biggest push there is.

"All right," Mo Yan says. She makes herself say it. "I am going to try something. If it goes wrong, I want you to know I am sorry."

She raises the bell.

---

She does not ring it.

She sets it, instead, against the stone girl's lifted hand, where the fingers curve toward her mouth, and holds it there. The glass is cold. For a moment nothing happens, and she thinks she has been a fool, and she thinks of the Ferryman's last grin and the way he said a girl of nine, as though the number were a joke he was telling her.

Then the bell begins to hum.

It is not a sound. She knows that at once, because she is listening for it and her ears hear nothing. It is a pressure behind her breastbone, a slow rising warmth, the way the moment before a song feels when the first note is already in your chest and has not yet been let out. The glass brightens at the center. A single point of cold white light, like a star at the bottom of black water, lifts and swells.

The stone girl's eyes move.

Mo Yan's heart stops. She keeps the bell where it is. She keeps her face still.

Please, she thinks, without meaning to, the way a person thinks a prayer. I am not afraid. I am not afraid of you. I am not afraid of the dark or the stone or the quiet. I am here. Please come out.

The light in the bell goes up her arm.

It is a feeling she does not have words for. It is like being poured out. Something warm and bright and enormous runs down her wrist, her elbow, her shoulder, through the center of her chest and out through the glass into the lifted stone hand, and as it goes it takes things with it. She feels it take the memory of the cart-house, and the cold, and the hospice smell of rue and tallow. She feels it take, and she cannot stop it, the shape of her mother's name.

Mama, she thinks, reaching for it, and there is a hole where the word was. A small, neat, clean hole.

She nearly lets go. Her fingers twitch on the glass. But the stone girl's lips, under the lifted hand, have begun to soften.

It happens slowly, the way ice goes soft at the edge of a pond. The gray falls out of her cheek. Color seeps into the lips, a flush of rose, the faintest tremor. The eyes blink, once. Then the lifted hand closes, trembling, around the bell and Mo Yan's own fingers, and the girl draws a breath so deep it makes her whole body shudder.

She does not speak.

She is, Mo Yan sees, terrified to. Her mouth is open and her throat is working and the tears are running down her stone-gray cheeks in two clean tracks, and she is holding her own voice in her chest with both hands, as Hua held the thought. She has been caught in the middle of a word for four days. She knows, better than anyone, what the Terrace does.

"It's all right," Mo Yan whispers. "You can whisper. Whispering is fine."

The girl shakes her head, hard.

"Then don't. Just stay." Mo Yan's hand is shaking. The bell is dimming. She feels the last of the warmth leave it and drain down into the stone, and the girl sways, and Mo Yan lets go of the glass and catches her around the ribs with both arms. "I've got you. I've got you."

The weight of her is enormous. It is the weight of a grown girl, half stone still from the knees down, and Mo Yan staggers and goes to one knee in the dust. They sit there together, the thin child and the girl in the blue robe, in the long shadow of the arch, while the bell lies in the dust beside them gone dark and quiet.

Thank you, the girl mouths.

Mo Yan nods.

What is your name?

She has to think about it. There is a hole where something should be, and she steps carefully around the edge of it, the way you step around a broken stair.

"Mo Yan," she says. "Mine's Mo Yan."

Lan, the girl mouths. Lan Xiu.

---

They do not go back to the shed at once.

Lan Xiu cannot walk. The stone in her legs has not gone, and it will not, Mo Yan can tell, without something more than one small bell. So she sits in the dust with her back against Mo Yan's shoulder, and the two of them watch the blue light go gray toward dawn.

It takes a long time for Lan Xiu to trust her hands. She flexes the fingers one at a time. She touches her braid, and finds it stone, and starts to cry again, silently, and Mo Yan sits with it. She has learned how to do that, over the past year. You do not say it will be all right. You sit. You let the weight rest against you. You do not leave.

After a while Lan Xiu begins to write.

She does it in the dust with one finger, in a quick, neat, scholar's hand, and Mo Yan reads each word as it forms.

Where is Elder Ye?

"Gone up. Three days ahead of us, the Cartographer says."

He left us.

"Yes."

The finger stops. Then, slowly: He did not want to. He cried. I saw it. She wipes the line away with her palm and writes again. The one in the gray robe made him go.

Mo Yan's skin crawls.

"What gray robe?"

The one who came down the stair behind him. Not the Cartographer. Taller. Wearing a hood. Lan Xiu's finger hesitates. No face. Just a ring on the hand. A circle with a gap. She looks up, and her eyes are enormous. She said that if Elder Ye stayed, we would all be stone. That she could not save all seven of us. That she could save one man, and he must be the one to go up.

Seven.

Mo Yan does the count in her head, because she has learned that counting keeps the floor under her feet. Six pupils on the Quay. Elder Ye. Seven.

"She chose him," she says.

She chose the one who could climb. Lan Xiu bites her lip. She said it was a kindness. That she was sorry.

"Veyra," Mo Yan whispers.

That is her name?

"I think so."

She is not a bad woman. The finger moves slowly. She wept too. I saw her hands shake. A pause. But she did not turn back.

---

By the time the light is full, Mo Yan has done something she did not plan.

She has gone down the line, kneeling at each of the five stone pupils in turn, and set the dark bell against each lifted hand. She had no right to try. She knows that. The first had cost her a name and a memory of her mother's voice, and she has nothing to spare. But the bell does not answer. At the second pupil it stays cold. At the third it stays cold. At the fourth it flickers and goes out.

It is spent, says a warm, creaking voice behind her. You gave it everything the first time.

She turns. The Cartographer is standing at the edge of the Quay with his gray cloak over his arm and a flat loaf of bread in his bandaged hand. He looks as though he has not slept in two hundred years, which Mo Yan supposes is nearly true. He is not rubbing his eyes. He is looking at the pale, living girl in the dust, and the expression on his broad face is a thing she has seen once, on the Ferryman, in the last second before he died.

You woke her, he says.

Mo Yan swallows. "I didn't know it would take—" She stops. Her mouth is dry. "I forgot something."

I know.

"My mother's name."

Yes. The Cartographer sets down the loaf and kneels, slowly, on creaking knees. His hand covers hers on the dead bell. That is the price of the Bell, little one. The Founders made it so. A bell that wakes the stone must be paid for in the thing the ringer loves best. It was Maren's rule, in the first days, to take a name. She took her own husband's. He closes his eyes. I should have told you. I did not think you would try.

"Is it gone? For good?"

I do not know. He is quiet. Names are strange. They hide. The Ferryman's little girl, the one in the bell, lost hers a hundred years before she lost anything else. And yet it was the first thing she remembered, on the last night. His thumb presses her knuckles. We shall see.

She nods. She does not cry. She finds, to her surprise, that she is angry, a small, hot, clear anger, like a coal in a clean hearth.

"Can the others be woken?"

Not with this. He lifts the bell and turns it in his scarred palm. The Bell has one fare in it. It is spent. But there is another way, and I think you have already guessed it.

She has.

"A voice that is not afraid," she says. "That's what you told Hua. The Keepers were waiting for a voice that is not afraid."

I told her that because I believed it. The Cartographer glances toward the great arch, where the long gray shadow of Veyra Thann is moving across the dust. Now I think it is more particular. I think it is a voice that is not afraid, and has paid. His gaze rests on the little girl in the blue robe. Lan Xiu has paid. She spent four days as stone, and came back with her mind. Her voice is a voice that knows the price. He sets the bell in Mo Yan's lap. If the others are woken, it will be by someone who has been where they are.

Lan Xiu, in the dust, stops writing.

She looks up at the Cartographer, and then at the line of her pupil-sisters on the Quay, and then, for a very long time, at Mo Yan.

I will, she writes. Her finger is steady. Tell me how.

---

Jian comes out of the shed at noon.

He takes in the scene without a word. The Quay. The living girl in the blue robe, propped against a sleeping Keeper, with a flat loaf and a cup of water at her side. The five stone pupils, still standing at the lip. Mo Yan sitting in the dust with the dark bell in her lap and a face so pale she looks like she has been rubbed with chalk.

"What did it cost?" he says.

She had known he would ask that. It is the first thing he always asks. She meets his gaze.

"A name."

He does not flinch. She thinks, in the weeks to come, that this is the thing she will remember best about him: that he never once flinched. He crouches in front of her, ruined hand tucked into his sleeve, and he says, very quietly, "Whose?"

"Mama's."

The silence between them is very long. Then he nods, once.

"I am sorry."

"It's not gone for good," she says quickly. "The Cartographer says names hide." She lifts her chin. "I'm going to find it."

"I know you are."

He looks past her, at the living girl. "Lan Xiu," he says. "Is that right?"

Yes, writes Lan Xiu in the dust.

"I am Lin Jian. I am a friend of the Wall, not the Sect. I want you to know that. I was not sent by Elder Ye, and I did not leave you here." He keeps his voice level. "I do not have the means to wake your sisters today. But I give you my word that I will come back. With the song, and with the time. If I live."

She studies him for a long moment, the dust-stained robe and the shaking hand and the tired eyes. Then she writes one word, and rubs it out, and writes another.

Why?

He considers it.

"Because there is a little girl under a lake," he says, "who thanked this one for a song. And because I think the people who built this road made a great mistake, and I think the mistake is still being made, and I would like to be someone who corrects it, and not someone who pays for it." He rises, slowly. "I would also like a great deal of tea."

Lan Xiu stares at him. And then she laughs.

It is soundless. It is a shaking of the shoulders, a gasp of air, a flash of white teeth, and it is the most beautiful thing Mo Yan has seen on the Terrace. It rolls across the Quay without a sound and the stone girl beside her, the one with the braid, does not so much as tremble. But the light in the Cartographer's face changes. And for the first time in eleven hours, Mo Yan feels the silence stop pressing, and just rest.

---

They lay it out at the table in the shed, over bread and bitter tea, with the lid of dark metal between them.

There are twenty-seven hours.

Jian says it flatly. He has the grain of salt on the table, still in the iron bowl, and the white slice of wood with the Cartographer's dotted bridge, and he says that nothing has been decided. He says that he will not take the Bridge. He says it without ceremony, before anyone asks, and Mo Yan sees Hua's shoulders ease.

"She does not know the cost," Jian says. "If she did, she would not agree. I do not intend to take what a person has not agreed to give."

Then we pay, Hua thinks. The shed carries it, as a faint bell-note. The fare. A year.

"A year each, if we all climb. Three years." Jian looks at Mo Yan. "I do not intend to take you above this Terrace."

"No," Mo Yan says.

"It is not a road for—"

"You said that about the last one, too." She puts the bell on the table. It is as dark as a pebble now. "You said it before the Ferryman. And he's dead, and I'm here, and I know things." She holds Jian's eyes. "I know what Veyra did. I know why Elder Ye left."

"Mo Yan—"

"She isn't lying." Her voice shakes, and she holds it steady. "That's the thing nobody's saying. She's not lying and she's not cruel. She chose Elder Ye over six children because it was the best she could do. And now she's going to choose the Wall over the Seam. She's been choosing for six hundred years. And she hates it." She swallows. "I don't think anyone has ever asked her to choose something else."

The shed is very quiet.

"Lan Xiu told you that?" Hua says.

"She watched Veyra's hands shake."

The Cartographer rubs his eyes. "Child," he says, with a kind of stunned tenderness, "you have just said the thing I have been trying to say for two hundred years."

Jian is looking at her with an expression she cannot name.

"If we can give her another choice," Mo Yan says, "she might take it."

"What other choice?"

She does not know. She says so. But the glass bell is in her lap, and the hole where her mother's name was is a small, cold place in her mind, and she thinks, with the clear plain logic that only a child who has lost something can have: a thing that has been paid for can be paid back.

"Take me to her," she says. "I want to talk."

---

Veyra Thann is standing in the arch when they come out, where she has stood for two days, a gray column against a paler sky. She turns her hooded head as the child crosses the dust. She does not move otherwise.

Mo Yan walks the whole hundred paces.

She does it with the bell in her left hand and her right hand open at her side, and she keeps her eyes on the hood, and she does not slow down. At ten paces she stops. At ten paces the woman could reach her in a stride.

She does not speak. She cannot, not aloud. She lifts the dark glass bell to the level of her heart and holds it out on her open palm, so the woman can see.

The hood tilts.

The Ferryman's bell, says a cool voice, in Hua's mind, and in Mo Yan's own, and in the quiet corner of the dust where Jian stands with his hand on a stone Keeper's shoulder. The first fare. I thought it had been lost.

It is not lost, Hua thinks, carrying the child's thought. She woke one of the Sect's pupils with it. It cost her her mother's name.

The woman in the arch is very still.

Then you have paid, says Veyra Thann. Her voice is quiet. You have paid the thing I paid. She lifts her bare hand, with the ring of ember light, and lets it fall. That is why you are not afraid of me.

I am a little afraid, Mo Yan thinks.

Good.

I want to ask you one thing.

Ask.

Is there anyone you would take back?

The Terrace holds its breath.

For a long time, nothing happens. The hooded figure does not move. The ring on her palm burns steady. Then, very slowly, the bandaged hand comes down from her breastbone, and the gray cloth parts at the wrist, and Mo Yan sees what has been hidden under it for six hundred years.

It is a bell.

Not black, like hers. White. It is made of some milky stone, no bigger than a plum, and set into the flesh of Veyra Thann's palm so deeply that the bone shows through. It is cracked down the center, a hairline of dark. A thin, steady light leaks from the crack, the color of the very first morning.

I would take back my daughter, says Veyra Thann, who is inside.

And Mo Yan, who has just lost her mother's name, who has stood in a cart-house in the dark and held a cloth over her own mouth, who has never once in her life been told that she is allowed to want something, lifts her small black bell, and holds it out across the dust toward the white one, and says, with her whole heart and not one sound:

Then let us find out what it costs.
